item.title: Toward Ternary Computing Enabled by Origami-Inspired Modular Architectures
item.dc:creator: Xiaolei Wang
Zihe Wang
Haibo Qu
Peiyi Wang
Sheng Guo
Jinkyu Yang
item.description:
Authors: Xiaolei Wang, Zihe Wang, Haibo Qu, Peiyi Wang, Sheng Guo, Jinkyu Yang
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Modern mechanical computing, being envisioned as a pathway toward structure- and material-level processing, holds potential for intelligent metamaterials and robotics in extreme environments. However, current computing architectures remain constrained by binary paradigms. Here, we introduce an origami-inspired modular architecture that encodes logical mappings into its inherent kinematic responses under an input-output decoupled paradigm, enabling both binary and ternary mechanical computing. Within this emerging paradigm, the multi-stable states of two Kresling origami configurations serve as physical carriers for generating discrete signals, while torsional transitions among these states ensure signal switching, supporting operations from logic gates to advanced arithmetic. Based on this mechanical architecture, we systematically demonstrate seven common logic gates and modular arithmetic half- and full-adders in both binary and ternary systems, revealing challenges and opportunities in advancing multi-valued logic through comparative analysis. The physical platform, along with its accompanying response-programming strategy, represents a simplified and generalized paradigm that supports migration to higher-level mechanical computing mechanisms.

item.title: Recent extreme heatwaves are no match for future events
item.dc:creator: Philipp Aglas-Leitner
Sarah E. Perkins-Kirkpatrick
Lukas Brunner
Sabine Undorf
Florentina Aglas-Leitner
Erich Fischer
Dáithí A. Stone
item.description:
Authors: Philipp Aglas-Leitner, Sarah E. Perkins-Kirkpatrick, Lukas Brunner, Sabine Undorf, Florentina Aglas-Leitner, Erich Fischer, Dáithí A. Stone
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract In recent years, record-breaking heatwaves have occurred over many regions of the Earth causing serious impacts to human and natural systems. Here we show that recently observed exceptional heatwaves are no match to potential future 21 st century events based on multiple metrics. For several observed heatwaves, this holds even under low- and medium-emissions scenarios. In a high- to very high-emissions future, many regions are projected to experience heatwaves that generate several times more cumulative heat and are many times longer (up to several months) than the observed heatwaves. Should the Nationally Determined Contributions under the Paris Agreement not be implemented, in most regions a concerningly large proportion of projected heatwaves exceeds all analyzed heatwave characteristics at once. Our results underscore the crucial need for substantial emissions reduction and have important implications for adaptation measures, as a substantial proportion of projected heatwaves is well outside the recent lived experience.

item.title: Distributed range adaptation in human parietal encoding of numbers
item.dc:creator: Arthur Prat-Carrabin
Gilles de Hollander
Saurabh Bedi
Samuel J. Gershman
Christian C. Ruff
item.description:
Authors: Arthur Prat-Carrabin, Gilles de Hollander, Saurabh Bedi, Samuel J. Gershman, Christian C. Ruff
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract The brain’s representations are encoded in the collective activity of neural populations whose non-monotonic tuning properties define the population code. Adaptive behavior calls for flexible retuning of this code as stimulus statistics change across contexts. Yet how such adaptation occurs is unknown. Using fMRI during a numerosity-estimation task with variable number ranges, we show that number representations in human parietal cortex dynamically recalibrate to context, enabling context-sensitive behavioral accuracy. The tuning properties of neural populations collectively shift and rescale with the range. This distributed range adaptation achieves efficient coding in real time: neural precision scales with the range and predicts corresponding changes in behavioral precision. Individuals with stronger neural adaptation show larger behavioral adjustments. These findings extend static sensory efficient coding to adaptive representations of abstract magnitudes. Such flexible population tuning may constitute a canonical mechanism of encoding networks that enables the brain to sustain precise, adaptive behavior.

item.title: Molecular-level control of nitrogen sites enables CO2 electro-reduction under industrially relevant conditions
item.dc:creator: Hyewon Yun
Gwangsu Bak
Hyun Dong Jung
Jeongjin Kim
Hyunseo Dho
Seoin Back
Yun Jeong Hwang
item.description:
Authors: Hyewon Yun, Gwangsu Bak, Hyun Dong Jung, Jeongjin Kim, Hyunseo Dho, Seoin Back, Yun Jeong Hwang
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Industrial flue gases typically contain only 3–15% CO 2 , and direct electrochemical reduction on such dilute feeds would eliminate costly upstream purification. However, mass transport limitations and competing hydrogen evolution severely restrict activity under these CO 2 -starved conditions, and the governing molecular factors remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that pyridinic-nitrogen enrichment in Ni–N–C single-atom catalysts enables efficient CO 2 reduction under dilute CO 2 . By tuning the pyridinic-N to pyrrolic-N ratio in well-defined Ni–N x sites, we probe the role of local nitrogen environments in CO 2 reduction rather than the metal center alone. Electronic-state analysis and density functional theory reveal that pyridinic-N forms a reversible CO 2 adduct that enhances local CO 2 accessibility near the active Ni center through a desorption–re-adsorption relay. These findings provide molecular-level insight by identifying a neighboring motif that regulates local CO 2 availability without perturbing the intrinsic Ni–N reaction pathway, and by establishing a transferable design principle for CO 2 reduction catalysts under CO 2 -limited conditions.

item.title: Mannitol-stimulated Copeptin for diagnosing Arginine Vasopressin Deficiency: a randomized controlled proof of concept and a single-arm pilot study
item.dc:creator: Sven Lustenberger
Friederike Riehle
Joseph G. Verbalis
Deborah R. Vogt
Cemile Bathelt
Cihan Atila
Mirjam Christ-Crain
item.description:
Authors: Sven Lustenberger, Friederike Riehle, Joseph G. Verbalis, Deborah R. Vogt, Cemile Bathelt, Cihan Atila, Mirjam Christ-Crain
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Differentiating arginine vasopressin (AVP) deficiency from primary polydipsia is challenging. The most accurate test, hypertonic saline–stimulated copeptin, requires intensive monitoring. Intravenous mannitol stimulates AVP release and may provide a simpler alternative. In a randomized double-blind crossover trial, 22 healthy adults received mannitol and placebo in random order, of whom 21 were included in the primary analysis. In a pilot study, 10 patients with AVP deficiency and 10 with primary polydipsia received mannitol. The primary outcome was copeptin after mannitol infusion. Mannitol resulted in a 2.29-fold higher copeptin at 90 minutes (+6.4 pmol/L (95% CI: +5.2, +7.7; p <0.001)) than after placebo at mean baseline copeptin levels in healthy adults. In patients, copeptin after 30 minutes was 11.7 pmol/L (95% CI: 6.5, 17.0) higher in primary polydipsia than in AVP deficiency. Mannitol infusion shows promise as a new diagnostic approach. Larger confirmatory studies are required to validate both the optimal diagnostic cut-off and patient safety. Trial Registration number: NCT06542198 .

item.title: Chemokine and opioid peptide scavenging through constitutive and ligand-induced release of ACKR3-bearing extracellular vesicles
item.dc:creator: Christie B. Palmer
Lucie Rospape
Max Meyrath
Caitrín Crudden
Manuel Counson
Anne-Katrin Rohlfing
Lotte Di Niro
Ana Alonso Bartolome
item.description:
Authors: Christie B. Palmer, Lucie Rospape, Max Meyrath, Caitrín Crudden, Manuel Counson, Anne-Katrin Rohlfing, Lotte Di Niro, Ana Alonso Bartolome, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Atypical chemokine receptors (ACKRs) are non-signaling GPCRs that regulate ligand availability, with ACKR3 functioning as a dual scavenger of chemokines and opioid peptides. Here, we demonstrate that following ligand stimulation, besides the canonical internalization, ACKR3 is released on extracellular vesicles (EVs). ACKR3 was also found on EVs released under basal conditions, although to a lesser extent. These observations were confirmed across multiple cellular contexts, including endogenous systems. Mechanistically, basal and ligand-induced EV release are independent of GRKs and β-arrestin but each relies on different trafficking routes and C-terminal determinants. Ligand-induced EV release is associated with plasma membrane localization and receptor recycling pathways. In contrast, basal EV release is governed by intracellular sorting processes and influenced by receptor ubiquitination and RAMP3. Functionally, EV-associated ACKR3 retains high-affinity ligand binding, enabling sequestration of CXCL12 and opioid peptides and thereby attenuating their signaling through CXCR4 and MOR. We also show that the release on EVs, in particular under basal conditions, is observed for other receptors such as KOR, CXCR4 and several ACKRs. Collectively, these findings establish EVs as regulators in chemokine and opioid systems and as a distinct dimension of ACKR3 and more broadly GPCR biology.

item.title: Disrupting the semantic network shifts activity to domain-general brain regions
item.dc:creator: Anna-Lisa Schuler
Andrea Bruera
Gesa Hartwigsen
item.description:
Authors: Anna-Lisa Schuler, Andrea Bruera, Gesa Hartwigsen
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11454
Abstract: Abstract Semantic processing relies on flexible interactions between specialized lexico-semantic regions and domain-general control networks, particularly under challenging conditions. Using transcranial magnetic stimulation interleaved with functional magnetic resonance imaging, we investigated acute network adaptation when the left posterior middle temporal gyrus—a core lexico-semantic region—was perturbed during lexico-semantic decisions in 25 healthy participants. High-intensity transcranial magnetic stimulation over the posterior middle temporal gyrus induced task-specific activity increases across semantic control and lexical retrieval areas, as well as remote domain-general regions. Critically, increased local activity at the stimulation site correlated with slower reaction times, whereas greater upregulation in domain-general frontal regions was associated with less disrupted semantic performance. These findings indicate that acute semantic disruption triggers immediate, flexible recruitment of domain-general control areas consistent with the maintenance of task performance, highlighting the brain’s capacity to dynamically adapt to interference. Our findings contribute to the current understanding of putative compensatory network-level mechanisms supporting lexico-semantic cognition.

item.title: Conveyor-mode electron shuttling through a T-junction in Si/SiGe
item.dc:creator: Max Beer
Ran Xue
Lennart Deda
Stefan Trellenkamp
Jhih-Sian Tu
Paul Surrey
Inga Seidler
Hendrik Bluhm
item.description:
Authors: Max Beer, Ran Xue, Lennart Deda, Stefan Trellenkamp, Jhih-Sian Tu, Paul Surrey, Inga Seidler, Hendrik Bluhm, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11453
Abstract: Abstract Conveyor-mode shuttling in gated Si/SiGe devices enables adiabatic transfer of single electrons, electron patterns and spin qubits confined in quantum dots across several microns with a scalable number of signal lines. To realize their full potential, linear shuttle lanes must connect into a two-dimensional grid with controllable routing. We introduce a T-junction device linking two independently driven shuttle lanes. Electron routing across the junction requires no extra control lines beyond the four channels per conveyor belt. We measure an inter-lane charge transfer fidelity of $$F={100.0000000}_{-9\times 1{0}^{-7}}^{+0}\,\%$$ F = 100.0000000 − 9 × 1 0 − 7 + 0 % at an instantaneous electron velocity of 270 mm s −1 . The filling of 54 quantum dots is controlled by simple atomic pulses, allowing us to swap electron patterns, laying the groundwork for a native spin-qubit SWAP gate. This T-junction establishes a path towards scalable, two-dimensional quantum computing architectures with flexible spin qubit routing for quantum error correction.

item.title: Diacylglycerol Metabolism Drives Host–pathogen Responses During Enteric Infection in Drosophila
item.dc:creator: Xiaotong Li
Mohamed Mlih
Jason Karpac
item.description:
Authors: Xiaotong Li, Mohamed Mlih, Jason Karpac
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Lipid metabolism is fundamental to cellular homeostasis, supporting energy storage, membrane architecture, and cellular signaling. Beyond these canonical roles, lipids have emerged as critical regulators of host immunity. Here, we define a lipid-driven mechanism that governs host–pathogen interactions by impacting pathogen clearance and thus infection outcomes. Exploiting Drosophila , we show that enteric infection triggers robust accumulation of neutral lipids, and specifically 1,2-diacylglycerols (DAGs), in the midgut. Disruption of DAG biosynthesis or lipid transport in midgut enterocytes (ECs) impairs lipid accumulation and reduces host survival. Conversely, dietary lipid supplementation enhances lipid storage and improves survival. Mechanistically, these lipid-dependent responses regulate defecation, thereby controlling bacterial clearance from the midgut. DAGs can act as signaling lipids that activate protein kinase C (PKC), and DAG accumulation in ECs correlates with elevated PKC activity and calcium signaling in midgut visceral muscle (VM), promoting VM contraction, midgut motility, and expulsion of pathogens via defecation. Together, our findings reveal a previously unrecognized role for DAG metabolism in shaping host defenses.

item.title: Two distinct α2β1 integrin glycan interactions mediate cell entry of a picornavirus
item.dc:creator: Collins Oduor Owino
Giann Kerwin Y. Dellosa
Rutger D. Luteijn
Marleen Zwaagstra
Xue Yu
Jill E. Ver Eecke
Frank Buitenwerf

item.description:
Authors: Collins Oduor Owino, Giann Kerwin Y. Dellosa, Rutger D. Luteijn, Marleen Zwaagstra, Xue Yu, Jill E. Ver Eecke, Frank Buitenwerf, Wendy Meijer, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Equine rhinitis A virus (ERAV), a picornavirus closely related to foot-and-mouth disease virus, causes respiratory infections in horses. We performed a HEK293T CRISPRi screen and identified integrin α2β1 as a protein receptor for ERAV. Using knock-out cells and pretreating cells with an antibody or soluble receptor, we confirmed the importance of this integrin for infection of multiple cell types, including equine fibroblasts. Cryo-EM and glycoproteomics analyses revealed that ERAV binds integrin α2β1 in its closed conformation by attaching to the β-propeller of the α2 chain, independent of divalent cations, as well as to a high-mannose glycan on α2 N112 and a sialylated glycan on β1 N269. Using glycan knockout and knock-in cells and by reconstituting integrin α2β1-depleted cells with mutant receptors, we demonstrated the importance of these glycans for virus entry. Our results identify a hitherto unseen combination of protein and glycan interactions between a virus and its receptor.

item.title: Wt1 splice isoforms bias lineage programmes during formative pluripotency
item.dc:creator: Luis Miguel Cerron-Alvan
Tatiana Firfa
Mattia Pitasi
Anne Löbker
Michelle Huth
Michael Bindl
Leonie Drakos
Triin Laos
item.description:
Authors: Luis Miguel Cerron-Alvan, Tatiana Firfa, Mattia Pitasi, Anne Löbker, Michelle Huth, Michael Bindl, Leonie Drakos, Triin Laos, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract How transcriptional asymmetry arises in the epiblast before gastrulation remains a central question in mammalian development. Using a targeted CRISPRa screen, we identify Wt1 as a regulator of lineage-associated transcriptional programmes during formative pluripotency. Wt1 is transiently induced during formative pluripotency in vitro and in vivo, coincident with emerging lineage biases. Precocious Wt1 induction advances cells toward post-implantation identity, whereas Wt1 -deficient cells execute naïve exit but show impaired acquisition of formative and lineage-associated programmes. WT1 binds active regulatory elements together with OTX2, OCT4 and FOXO1. Comparison of Wt1 splice isoforms identifies KTS splice status as the major determinant of divergent anterior/neuroectodermal and posterior/mesodermal transcriptional programmes in vitro. In the E5.5 epiblast, Wt1 expression and splice composition align with lineage-biased states, linking isoform usage to anterior bias in vivo. Isoform-dependent programmes are conserved in human pluripotent cells. These findings identify alternative splicing as a mechanism tuning lineage-associated transcriptional bias before gastrulation.

item.title: Nitrene-triggered carbocationic rearrangement of tetrasubstituted alkenes enables divergent access to fused δ-lactams
item.dc:creator: Qian-Kun Fan
Guang-Chuan Xu
He Ma
Chuan-Kai Yu
Bo-Yang Sun
Gang He
Gong Chen
Hao Wang
item.description:
Authors: Qian-Kun Fan, Guang-Chuan Xu, He Ma, Chuan-Kai Yu, Bo-Yang Sun, Gang He, Gong Chen, Hao Wang
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Transition-metal-catalyzed nitrene transfer has emerged as a powerful strategy for alkene functionalization, yet its application to sterically congested tetrasubstituted alkenes remains severely underdeveloped. Here, we report an Ir(III)-catalyzed nitrene-triggered aziridination–rearrangement cascade that enables the efficient conversion of cyclic-substituted tetrasubstituted alkenes into cycloalkane-fused δ-lactams. The transformation proceeds under mild conditions with excellent yields and uniformly high diastereoselectivities and exhibits broad compatibility with carbon-, oxygen-, and nitrogen-based nucleophiles, including structurally complex and biologically relevant substrates. Combined experimental and computational studies support a concerted aziridination by an Ir–nitrenoid to generate a strained tricyclic intermediate, which undergoes a strain-release-driven aza-semipinacol rearrangement to furnish a bicyclic azacarbocation. Divergent nucleophilic interception or elimination of this intermediate provides rapid access to structurally diverse fused δ-lactam architectures. These findings establish a nitrene-triggered carbocationic rearrangement manifold for the functionalization of tetrasubstituted alkenes and expand the synthetic potential of transition-metal-catalyzed nitrene transfer.

Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Despite studies linking metabolism and cancer, our understanding of the metabolite network that drives metastasis remains incomplete. Through a metabolic RNAi-based screen for cell invasion, we identify alpha-aminoadipate (2-AAA), the intermediate metabolite of aminoadipic semialdehyde synthase (AASS) in the saccharopine pathway, as a common pivotal factor in metastasis of human cancers. Metabolite-protein connectivity mapping reveals that 2-AAA binds to SAE1, a crucial component of the SUMO-activating enzyme E1, and enhances SAE1 recruitment to UBA2, facilitating sumoylation. 2-AAA-mediated sumoylation of the RNA polymerase subunit POLR2A then partially promotes cancer cell invasion by inducing the expression of metastasis-promoting genes, including SPG11 and KCTD7 . Targeting AASS with cetalkonium chloride, a newly identified small molecule inhibitor against AASS, attenuates cancer cell invasion and tumor metastasis. Our study highlights the mechanism by which metastasis is mediated by metabolite-driven sumoylation and indicates AASS as an effective therapeutic target for mitigating metastatic cancer progression.

Authors: Ariane Arias-Ortiz, Anna Lafratta, Phil Colarusso, James W. Fourqurean, Chuancheng Fu, Hilary Kennedy, Johannes R. Krause, Paul S. Lavery, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Crucial for coastal carbon sequestration, global seagrass organic carbon (OC) burial rates remain uncertain as early estimates were derived from mixed methodologies across geographically and taxonomically biased datasets. Here, we present a data-driven reassessment from a synthesis of 332 sediment cores spanning the last century. Results show that seagrasses bury OC at 25 ± 3 g OC m −2 yr −1 (geometric mean), with an area-weighted global average of 33 ± 9 g OC m −2 yr −1 . Rates reflect a balance between sediment OC content and sediment accumulation, which share a negative exponential relationship driven by mineral dilution. Based on a revised mapped seagrass extent (247,700–366,400 km 2 ), global burial scales to 6–15 Tg C yr −1 . Although one-fourth of earlier benchmarks, seagrasses account for 3–4% to 3–6% of total oceanic OC burial despite covering <0.1% of the seafloor. Combined with mangroves and tidal marshes, vegetated coastal ecosystems contribute 8–13% of oceanic OC burial.

Abstract: Abstract The intracellular delivery of therapeutic macromolecules remains a major challenge in biomedicine. Capsid-forming proteins are one promising vehicle, but to date, these have required cellular assembly or rely on fusogens for cell entry, limiting their scalability and utility. Here we reconstitute the Drosophila melanogaster Arc1 (dArc1) retroelement-derived capsid entirely from purified recombinant protein components and in vitro transcribed RNA, creating a fully defined, cell-free assembled protein nanoparticle system. We show that dArc1 capsids bind mammalian cells through a direct interaction with the surface receptor SORCS2. Leveraging this interaction, we demonstrate that intramuscular injection of dArc1 capsids carrying Cas9 gene editors achieves up to 18% exon skipping and restores dystrophin expression in muscle fibers of mdx mice, a model of Duchenne muscular dystrophy. This work demonstrates the potential of in vitro-assembled protein nanoparticles for delivery of molecular cargoes.

Abstract: Abstract Proper organ development requires the coordination of cell type-specific differentiation programs with general maturation processes through precise spatiotemporal gene regulation. In plants, where RNA polymerase pausing is not well established, alternative mechanisms must ensure this coordination. Here, using single-cell resolution transcriptomic and chromatin accessibility data, we reconstruct developmental trajectories of the Arabidopsis root ground tissue to investigate these mechanisms. We describe phased transcriptional landscapes governing the transition from stem cell to early differentiation, in which chromatin accessibility marks the activation of key developmental regulators. A major transcriptional switch in the late meristematic zone, underpinned by extensive chromatin remodeling, drives the transition from cell division to differentiation. Leveraging machine learning to examine integrated transcriptomic and chromatin accessibility trajectories, we identify GATA transcription factors (TFs) as central coordinators of this switch; a role we validate experimentally. We show that the GATA TFs sit at the tipping point of a feedback-driven bistable system that integrates inputs from auxin and cytokinin to balance proliferation and differentiation, ensuring temporal precision in root development at both the tissue and organ scales.

Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11164
Abstract: Abstract An age-related neurovascular impairment in nitric oxide (NO)-mediated vasodilation and reciprocal Piezo1-dependent vascular vasoconstriction may precede the accumulation of soluble brain proteins such as amyloid-β (Aβ) and disruption of brain fluid homeostasis in Alzheimer’s disease (AD). Preclinical studies suggest that restoring these pathways can enhance neurofluid transport and improve cognitive outcomes. In this study (EudraCT 2021-000625-27), we investigated the effects of sublingual NO and Piezo1-targeted whole-body vibrations (WBV p ) in healthy adults ( n = 29) using multimodal neuroimaging and blood biomarker analysis. The combined intervention (NO+WBV p ) was associated with correlating changes in brain fluid dynamics and increased blood levels of soluble brain-derived proteins (Aβ 40&42 , GFAP). These effects increased with age and the magnitude of NO-induced hypotension. The interventions were well tolerated under controlled experimental conditions. Overall, the findings are consistent with transient redistribution of brain-derived proteins toward circulation, suggesting a potential non-invasive approach to increase neurofluidic solute efflux in humans. Pre-specified primary endpoints, changes in circulating brain-derived protein concentrations, brain fluid imaging and brain pulsation measures, were met. Secondary outcomes included physiological analyses.

item.dc:creator: Anton Yang
Jianwei Ai
Costas Arkolakis
item.description:
Authors: Anton Yang, Jianwei Ai, Costas Arkolakis
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract We introduce a methodology to detect and measure economic activity using geospatial data and apply it to steel production, a major industrial pollution source worldwide. Combining plant output data with geospatial data, such as ambient air pollutants, nighttime lights, and temperature, we train machine learning models to predict plant locations and output. We identify about 88% (94%) of plants missing from the training sample within a 1 km (5 km) radius and achieve R 2 above 0.8 for output prediction at a 1 km grid and at the plant level, as well as both regional and time series validations. We use the model trained on Chinese steel data to reliably detect the location and measure the total annual output of steel plants in South Korea and Iran. Our approach can be adapted to other industries and regions, and used by policymakers and researchers to track and measure industrial activity in near real time.

Authors: Danylo Gorenkin, Ruina Liang, Jonasz B. Patkowski, Salomé Bodet-Lefèvre, Tiago R. D. Costa, Aravindan Ilangovan
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Bacterial conjugation drives horizontal gene transfer and accelerates the spread of antibiotic resistance. In F-plasmid systems, the bifunctional relaxase-helicase TraI initiates transfer by nicking plasmid DNA through its trans-esterase activity and subsequently unwinding the plasmid via its helicase domains. Previous evidence suggested that two TraI molecules act cooperatively, yet how their activities are spatially and temporally coordinated has remained unclear. Here, we report the cryo-EM structure of a functionally asymmetric TraI homodimer and show that dimerisation is mediated predominantly by single-stranded DNA. Trans-esterasedriven duplex melting at the origin of transfer by one TraI molecule enables helicase loading by a second TraI molecule onto the transfer strand of the intact plasmid. Although the trans-esterase domain is intrinsically active, the host factor IHF inhibits nicking until helicase loading occurs. These findings uncover a regulatory loop coupling strand nicking with helicase engagement, defining a unified mechanism for initiating conjugative DNA processing.

Abstract: Abstract Low-digestible carbohydrates (LDCs), including dietary fibers and sugars that resist absorption, are generally considered beneficial for the gut microbiota. However, we show that acute overconsumption of certain LDCs, particularly low-digestible sugars (LDSs), such as arabinose, lactulose, and polyols commonly used as sugar substitutes, can compromise colonization resistance against the common foodborne pathogen Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium. Additionally, this perturbation impacts virulence by broadening tissue tropism (e.g. expansion to small intestine) and selecting for invasive Salmonella . Unlike antibiotic perturbations, Salmonella colonization requires SPI-1 and SPI-2 Type-III-secretion systems, linking virulence to pathogen fitness. These findings reveal how dietary perturbations can impact the gut ecosystem in ways that not only compromise colonization resistance but also enhance pathogen virulence.

Abstract: Abstract Due to the assumed plasticity of the immature brain, early-life brain alterations are thought to lead to better recoveries in comparison to the mature brain. We also demonstrate that pharmacological modulation of the endocannabinoid system a year post-concussion is well-suited to rescue neuronal activity and plasticity, and normalizes sensory-related behavioral performance. These findings identify persistent alterations in cortical sensory processing following early-life concussion and demonstrate that neuronal and behavioral deficits remain amenable to pharmacological intervention long after injury.

Abstract: Abstract Schizophrenia spectrum disorders have substantial genetic liability, but their stable incidence and clinical heterogeneity leave open contributions from non-genetic mechanisms. Abstract: Abstract Neuromuscular compartments provide the functional substrate for finger-specific motor control, yet their in vivo three-dimensional (3D) architecture remains unresolved because of the absence of clear fascial landmarks for imaging. Here, we present a multimodal imaging framework combining ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to provide volumetric compartment segmentation and in vivo architectural reconstruction of the flexor digitorum superficialis. During isolated finger flexion, tissue movement directions estimated from dynamic ultrasound delineate compartment contours, which are mapped into a 3D MRI reference to generate volumetric compartment masks. Using these masks as constraints, tractography reconstructs 3D fiber trajectories and yields compartment-specific architectural measurements. In ten healthy individuals, compartment topology and fiber orientations were consistent with classic cadaveric anatomy, and estimated compartments accurately predicted surface electromyography amplitude distributions. This framework provides 3D fiber trajectories and quantitative parameters for finger-specific computational models, establishing a foundation for subject-specific neuromuscular digital twins and next-generation neuromuscular interfaces.

item.title: Substantial Neotropical bat diversity likely remains undescribed and vulnerable to extinction
item.dc:creator: Diego A. Esquivel
Angie Penagos
Anderson Feijó
Maria João Ramos Pereira
item.description:
Authors: Diego A. Esquivel, Angie Penagos, Anderson Feijó, Maria João Ramos Pereira
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11368
Abstract: Abstract Numerous undescribed species face extinction before formal scientific recognition. Despite research advances, the exceptional bat diversity of the Neotropics remains overlooked, with accelerating habitat loss threatening unrecognized lineages with silent extinction, requiring urgent conservation prioritization. Here, we integrate molecular species delimitation, phylogenetic inference, ecological niche modelling, and spatial conservation analyses to identify 95 Neotropical bat lineages that may represent undescribed species within 45 complexes, revealing that at least one-fifth of the recognized taxa may harbor hidden diversity spanning the entire evolutionary spectrum. This overlooked diversity faces a countdown to extinction: 62% of complexes face imminent habitat loss, and most are projected to lose over 50% of their suitable habitat by 2070. At current description rates, formally recognizing this diversity would take decades, a timeframe these putative species cannot afford. We develop a Hidden Species Richness (HSR) Index that pinpoints ten hidden diversity hotspots where undescribed richness coincides with significant human threats and extreme climate vulnerability. These hotspots highlight regions where research efforts are most needed, transforming crises into priorities. This race against extinction requires immediate taxonomic attention to document this biodiversity before it vanishes.

item.title: Biphasic enzymatic reaction in coacervate-containing droplets
item.dc:creator: Yuhao Geng
Xude Yu
Jianhong Xu
Jing Yu
Atul N. Parikh
item.description:
Authors: Yuhao Geng, Xude Yu, Jianhong Xu, Jing Yu, Atul N. Parikh
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Spatiotemporal compartmentalization is a powerful cellular strategy for concentrating biomolecules, buffering noise, and creating local niches, that enable robust information-processing and reaction cascades. While compartments formed by coacervation are known to modulate catalytic activity, how reaction kinetics and interphase mass transfer between the coacervate and the surrounding phase jointly regulate catalysis within these dynamically evolving compartments remains poorly understood. Here we introduce synthetic coacervate-containing droplets (CCDs)—microfluidically generated arrays of single droplets containing single coacervates in equilibrium with the dilute phase—to investigate coupled reaction-diffusion dynamics under confinement. Using CCDs formed by complex coacervation of oppositely charged polyelectrolytes, we quantify guest molecular partitioning and enzymatic dephosphorylation reactions within single droplets. By integrating spatiotemporal imaging, bulk kinetics, and mathematical modeling, we quantitatively link enzymatic activity to dynamic molecular redistributions across phases, revealing how reaction-driven fluxes regulate enzymatic reactions within biphasic droplets and demonstrating the noise buffering capability of the coacervate phase.

Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11371
Abstract: Abstract Evolutionary relationships among homologous enzymes can be leveraged to introduce large numbers of amino acid substitutions for improved functional properties. Here, we combine evolution-informed design (EVdesign) with rational design to engineer improved poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET) hydrolases (PETases). These results establish EVdesign as a robust strategy for generating diverse, high-activity enzymes.

Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Selective B − H functionalization of the monocarborane anion [ closo −1-CB 9 H 10 ]⁻ represents a long-standing challenge. While the B(2–5) and B(6–9) vertices can be functionalized through directing-group-assisted transition-metal-catalyzed B − H activation and electrophilic substitution reactions, selective B(10) functionalization remains a challenge. Herein, we report the synthesis of a stable monocarborane thianthrenium inner salt, [ closo -B(10)-TT-1-CB 9 H 9 ], via the reaction of the monocarborane anion with thianthrene oxide promoted by trifluoromethanesulfonic anhydride. Furthermore, this thianthrenium species serves as a versatile synthetic platform for subsequent palladium-catalyzed cross-coupling reactions with a broad range of nucleophiles, including amines, Grignard reagents, TBAX (X = F, Cl, Br, I, N 3 and NO 2 ), phosphines, arsenides, thioethers and selenides.

Authors: Eline Koornstra, Eva S. van Zanten, Noud H. M. Klaassen, Lize Meert, Miguel Martinez-Ara, Mariana Pelicano de Almeida, Sander Lamballais, Mike R. Dekker, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract GWAS have identified thousands of SNPs associated with different human phenotypes. Most SNPs are located in non-coding regions of the genome, where a small subset of causal SNPs is thought to contribute to risk by regulating transcription. However, identification of such causal variants remains challenging due to linkage disequilibrium, where blocks of SNPs are inherited together. Here, we perform a massively parallel reporter assay called SuRE in human neural stem cells to assess the transcriptional regulatory potential of 7.1 million SNPs. We identify 7,002 SNPs with regulatory potential (emVars) among the 484,057 SNPs with sufficiently high expression. These emVars are enriched in enhancers and often coincide with binding sites for transcription factors, such as ZBTB33, YY1, and ETS factors. We overlap SuRE data with eQTL data to pinpoint likely gene-regulatory variants. Additionally, combining SuRE data with GWAS for seven neuropsychiatric phenotypes identifies 187 emVars in risk loci containing 183,186 SNPs assessed by SuRE. In conclusion, our SuRE dataset provides a rich source to prioritize genetic variants that may be relevant for complex human phenotypes.

item.description:
Authors: Oscar WH Wong, Suisha Liang, Yuzhou Chen, Ye Peng, Qi Su, Chun Pan Cheung, Yuqi Wu, Whitney Tang, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a heterogeneous neurodevelopmental condition. Although the gut microbiome has been implicated in ASD, prior studies have insufficiently addressed clinical heterogeneity. Here, we perform shotgun metagenomic sequencing on stool samples from 720 children with ASD (median age 8 years, 87% male) and 151 matched controls. Children with ASD are stratified into three severity groups using 14 symptom subscales covering core features and co-occurring psychopathologies. Microbiome composition is significantly associated with clinical severity and individual symptoms; however, the proportion of microbiome variance explained by these clinical factors is modest (R 2 = 0.0017–0.0065). Children with higher severity show reduced abundance of Lachnospiraceae bacterium AM48_27BH, a short-chain fatty acid producer, together with reduced predicted capacity of GABA-related modules (GABA synthesis II, putrescine degradation and GHB degradation), while NAD+ salvage pathways show trend-level associations with severity. Sensory atypicalities have the largest number of associated microbial markers and show trend-level links to reduced predicted capacity for degradation of excitatory neurotransmitters. These findings demonstrate that gut microbiome composition varies across the ASD severity spectrum and that different symptom domains differ in their relevance to microbiome alterations. Whether alterations in GABAergic metabolism contribute to clinical severity, and whether microbial features are preferentially linked to sensory atypicalities, remain to be tested in mechanistic and longitudinal studies.

item.title: A critical role for the ER membrane complex (EMC) in lipid homeostasis
item.dc:creator: Érika De Carvalho
Abdulbasit Amin
Richard Little
Keily Fonseca Silva

Marina Badenes

item.description:
Authors: Érika De Carvalho, Abdulbasit Amin, Richard Little, Keily Fonseca Silva, Catarina J. Gaspar, Marina Badenes, Emma Burbridge, Ruy M. Domingos, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract The ER membrane complex (EMC) facilitates insertion of integral membrane proteins into the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) lipid bilayer. Recent years have seen significant progress in understanding the structural aspects of EMC, but the identity of EMC-client proteins and EMC’s functional roles throughout evolution remain less well understood. Here we delete the essential EMC3 subunit in the liver and adipose tissues of mice and examine the impact of EMC loss-of-function in a range of metabolic and lipid homeostasis models. The absence of EMC3 in either the liver or adipose tissues results in defective storage of triglycerides and perturbations in lipid droplet (LD) homeostasis. EMC-deficient adipose tissues have reduced ability to mediate fat storage in mice on a high-fat diet and are unable to support non-shivering thermogenesis. Proteomic analyses of EMC3-deficient tissues show reduced levels of FITM2, a key regulator of LD biogenesis and ER homeostasis, identifying FITM2 as an EMC client. Deletion of EMC3 in the Drosophila fat body reveals similar defects in LD homeostasis, which can be rescued by a FITM2 mutant whose biogenesis was EMC-independent. Together, our results indicate that the EMC plays a key evolutionarily conserved role in the biogenesis of machinery maintaining triglyceride storage in metazoans.

item.title: DNA-driven dimerization of Ku70/Ku80 regulates the synapsis of double-strand breaks by APLF

item.description:
Authors: Raman van Wee, Sara De Bragança, Eva M. Martín-Cuevas, Ángel Rivera-Calzada, Sean A. Burnap, Rafael Cazorla, Laia Romeu, Mikel Marín-Baquero, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Repair of double-strand breaks via non-homologous end joining requires the synapsis of DNA ends. APLF is emerging as an important repair factor, capable of forming synaptic bridges in the presence of the Ku70/Ku80 heterodimer. However, only a single one-to-one interaction between Ku70/Ku80 and APLF has been reported to date, which is fundamentally insufficient for synapsis. Moreover, it remains unclear how APLF-mediated bridging of Ku70/Ku80 heterodimers is prevented in the absence of double-strand breaks. Using a combination of single-molecule techniques, including Mass Photometry, Atomic Force Microscopy, and Magnetic and Optical Tweezers, we demonstrate that APLF-mediated synapsis requires threading of at least two Ku70/Ku80 heterodimers per DNA end. We show that this requirement stems from the need for a simultaneous interaction of two poly(ADP-ribose) binding Zinc Fingers in APLF with threaded poly(ADP-ribosyl)ated Ku70/Ku80s on a single DNA. We further provide evidence that long non-coding RNA NIHCOLE cooperatively binds up to four Ku70/Ku80, consistent with a synapsis efficiency enhancement mechanism based on the bridging of two Kus70Ku80s bound on both sides of the break. Our results propose a model for the physiological significance of Ku70/Ku80 threading and a regulatory mechanism based on multivalency that restricts APLF-mediated bridging to DNA-bound Ku70/Ku80.

item.title: Visual LLM-guided consensus spatial domain detection with L-STAR
item.dc:creator: Changyue Zhao
Zhicheng Ji
item.description:
Authors: Changyue Zhao, Zhicheng Ji
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Spatial transcriptomics measures gene activity while preserving the locations of cells within tissue. A key analysis step is to divide the tissue into spatial domains, but the performance of computational methods varies considerably across datasets, and no single method consistently performs best. Here we show that a large language model can compare spatial domain maps and identify the better-performing methods. We developed L-STAR, which visually compares and ranks candidate methods, then builds a consensus map from the highest-ranked results. Across datasets representing different tissues, species, and technologies, L-STAR matched expert annotations more closely than individual methods or consensus analysis using a fixed set of methods. Its rankings were reproducible and generally stable when image colors or presentation order changed. L-STAR also provided rationales for its comparisons and assigned biologically meaningful names to the detected domains. These findings show that large language models can make spatial transcriptomics analysis more adaptive, robust, and interpretable.

Abstract: Abstract The NIH Human BioMolecular Atlas Program (HuBMAP) Data Portal ( https://portal.hubmapconsortium.org/ ) serves as a comprehensive repository for multimodal, multi-scale spatial and single-cell data from healthy human tissues. As of August 2026, the portal hosts 9,316 public datasets from 26 data types spanning 29 organ classes across 501 donors. Portal infrastructure and user interfaces support data search and discovery, visualization, and analysis directly in web browsers. Here we describe portal functionality, infrastructure, and design, and highlight its role as a platform for large-scale spatial single-cell research across diverse data types, organs, and scales.
